utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all the participants in the proceedings. Before we proceed, I should like to enter a correction in yesterday's transcript. At the very end of the testimony, when I asked Mr. Sljivancanin about the talk that he had with Colonel Mrksic, which is page 87 of the working transcript, from line 2 to line 17, Mr. Sljivancanin first spoke in the first person and then in the third person. So in order not to read the entire passage, we, in the courtroom, are quite clear on who was saying what and what Mr. Mrksic was being saying and what was being interpreted by Mr. Sljivancanin. So from line 5 to line 17, there should be quotation marks only in that passage, which is the portion where Mr. Sljivancanin quotes the words of Mr. Mrksic. If there is any dispute about that, I shall ask Mr. Sljivancanin to repeat. When he says, "I had a talk with the principal, with the directress of the hospital, he is obviously interpreting the words, relaying the words, of Mr. Mrksic. I believe that there is no doubt about that so that there is no need to ask Mr. Sljivancanin any further clarifying questions. The second thing I should like to say has to do with --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic looking at me. The only thing that I would have suggested, with the utmost of respect, it's probably wiser and more prudent for Mr. Sljivancanin to be asked the question again and we know exactly then what is being said, rather than speculating. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, let us then clarify this first. Will you tell us what Mr. Mrksic told you when you returned to Negoslavci, having toured Vukovar with Mr. Vance. But when you speak, don't speak in the first person, or do specify when you are quoting, for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning all. Upon finishing -- the finish of the visit by Mr. Vance, I returned to the command post. I reported to the commander that Vance had left our zone with the delegation. On that occasion, Commander Mrksic told me that the units of the 1st Militarised Battalion had passed across the bridges on the River Vuka and had entered the sector where the buildings of the Vukovar Hospital and of the Vukovar MUP were. He said that he had talked with the director, lady director, of the hospital and that he had promised help to the hospital. He said that -- he asked me, he actually asked me, to look for and find the representatives of the International Red Cross, with whom I was frequently cooperating, and to see how much medical supplies they could give to the hospital and to take them there. And he also told me to see whether there were any of our soldiers, captured soldiers there. He told me to analyse security issues, which I'm not going to enumerate right now, and I believe that he said to me that General Zivota Panic -- or that I was to call him by phone, or he actually told me personally that I should look for Dr. Gordana Antic in the hospital and to send her on the first transport, as quickly as possible, to Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prior to proceeding with the examination, two other matters which I still have to clarify from yesterday related to Mr. Sljivancanin's answers from the beginning of the session, as far as his perception of the OG South is concerned. And we asked Witness Trifunovic, on the 5th of May, 2006; the pages in the transcript are 8332 and 8333. I also asked representatives of the OTP, as this morning we received another four translations into the B/C/S language from them, whether they can personally give those documents to Mr. Sljivancanin - yes, I see that they are ready - so that he can familiarise himself with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Sljivancanin, now I'm talking to you, I suppose that you also would like us to efficiently transact this business, deal with this part today, so please be so kind as to give us very precise and brief answers so that we can deal with these topics which are highly relevant to your defence. So give us brief descriptions and just give us the material, the important things. So my next question is: What did you do after that? Where did you go, and did you go with someone?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the sector of my building in Negoslavci and I issued a task that Mr. Borsinger be found. When he was found, I had a talk with him in which he said that currently he had a small lorry with medical supplies and that he could help me out with that and that we should go to the hospital. So we agreed and we set out towards the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Together?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in my vehicle, he was in his vehicle, and there was this small lorry, so it was a small column.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before we go on, one question: You heard the testimony given before this Court to the effect that approximately on that day, at that time, there was a meeting in Negoslavci. You saw written evidence between Colonels Pavkovic and Loncar and Misevic and Mr. Kypr and Mr. Schou, i.e., these two representatives of the European Community. Tell me briefly, were you at that meeting? Did you know that that meeting was being held in Negoslavci at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not attend that meeting. The first time I learned about that meeting having been held was when I came here to the Detention Unit and when I received materials from the OTP and heard testimonies of the witnesses Kypr and Schou here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, on the 19th of November, have any direct or any other contact through signals communication with representatives of the European Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, I only had encounters with the delegation that came with Mr. Vance and with Mr. Borsinger. As regards other European monitors or ICRC representatives, no, I had no contacts with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, and if so, ever hear of the Zagreb agreement here in this courtroom of the 18th of November which was concluded between Mr. Hebrang and Raseta?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that agreement for the first time here in the Tribunal, at The Hague, and I saw it here for the first time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the developments in Vukovar, did you know that there was some negotiations being conducted in Zagreb, the outcome of which was that agreement? Had anybody informed you about that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I had never heard about those negotiations. At the time, I was just the chief of security of the Guards Brigade and I had no way of knowing about such negotiations being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When, approximately, did you arrive at the hospital? What time of day was it? And what happened thereafter? Whom did you see?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived at the hospital, after having to negotiate the obstacles on the road which were being cleared by engineer machinery. As far as I can recall, it was in the afternoon. Whether it was 3.00 or 4.00 p.m., I cannot say with precision, but it was definitely one hour prior to nightfall, because one could see; there was visibility. At the gate to the hospital, at the entrance to the yard of the hospital, I met with the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion, Major Borivoje Tesic, and the commander of the 2nd Military Police Battalion, Radoje Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radoje Paunovic is the name of the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the military police. They briefed me very briefly that the commander of the military police had been given the task by the commander to assume security; that there were many civilians in the hospital; that they had found outfits, clothing, equipment, bombs, weapons, in and outside the hospital; and they drew my attention to the fact that I should not go into the cellars or the corridors of the hospital because it wasn't safe until full security measures were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "clothing," what did you mean? What did they find?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They found, and they showed me, camouflage uniforms, soldiers' camouflage uniforms. Mr. Borsinger was with me all the time. I don't remember that he had an interpreter at the time; I don't know whether he understood it all, everything that we were saying. But I do know that both I and Mr. Borsinger suggested that civilians should go to Velepromet so that they would be assigned to the different centres or to places where they should be. And they told me that they had found a shelter where the staff of the National Guards Corps and their commander was, that it was mined; and they also told me that they had found large numbers of bodies, of corpses, human corpses, in another street, in a street opposite the hospital. They proposed that they take me to the office of the hospital lady director, and from there we went to the cellar together, to the entrance which is quite well known, the one where the wounded were taken in and out of the hospital, and we went straight to the office of Mrs. Vesna Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were speaking in plural. Who was with you all the time? Let us be precise.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Tesic, Major Paunovic, and Mr. Borsinger were with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can go on.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I took a very hard -- I was introduced to Madam Bosanac. I asked her if she was faced with any problems and I told her that we had brought medicaments for the hospital. I also asked her whether -- I said, "Are there any of our soldiers here?" Mrs. Vesna Bosanac, more or less, said this to me, in answering, she said that contrary to her approval, a large number of civilians had arrived at the hospital, as well as other people whom she didn't know, and she said that this was obstructing their further work of treatment of the wounded. She said that there were three of our soldiers at the hospital, that they were undergoing treatment and that if I wanted, I could see them. Then I asked her if she knew that civilians were supposed to go to Velepromet, to which she responded that she knew that and that she had drawn their attention to that and that it was precisely there that some women were. And she actually introduced a woman to me whose name, however, I've forgotten and cannot recall at this point. She introduced her as an activist of the Red Cross who was working on having the civilians led in an organised fashion from the hospital to Velepromet for the purpose of the further evacuation. After that, we went to see our soldiers. When one goes out of her office - and I remember that very well - we took the lift in the corridor, because the office is right at the entrance to the cellars of that building. So we took a lift [as interpreted] corridor, arrived at a large room which was full of wounded people, among whom I recognised also Sergeant Ljubic [as interpreted]. I said hello to him and the other two soldiers and another two soldiers. Mrs. Vesna Bosanac was there as well. Tesic might also have been with me, but I know for a fact that Borsinger did not enter that room. On that occasion Jovic told me, he said, "Comrade Major, please don't go any further. There is a large number of masked members of the National Guards Corps here," and he pointed to a corner where there were three people in white overalls and he said that they were disguised. He said that people also had weapons, in particular, bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, the 17th line, it says "lift corridor" and you said "left corridor." You said "Sergeant Jovic" and it is "Ljubic" in the transcript. I believe that was later corrected. And the quotation marks are properly placed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can go on.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we stayed there for a short time. It was very difficult. It was very distressing for me, especially having to see so many wounded people and seeing that we had all those problems that we have gone through together. So I returned with Mrs. Vesna Bosanac again to her office. In front of the door, there was already a group of people waiting, a group of men and women in white coats waiting. They all wanted to know when the evacuation would be and all of them wanted to say something to me. So all of them had something to tell me. For the most part, what they were telling me, first, there were people that were saying they wanted to cooperate with the JNA, that they were hiding at the hospital --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, sorry, interpreter's correction: That members of the National Guards Corps and of the MUP were hiding at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never helped them. And even some weapons had been introduced into the hospital. At that time I met a man, whose name I did not remember at the time, who introduced himself as the director of surgery - this is what he said - and he said that he had performed surgery on our soldiers, that he had helped them, and that he wanted to help. And he also added that pressure had been exerted on him; that the night before he had to dress wounds and put dressings on healthy people and plaster casts and that he would be showing to us who these people were. Later in the morning, when I arrived, I found that his name was Dr. Njavro Gjuro, or rather, Gjuro Njavro. I told him, "Okay, we are going to discuss this." I wanted to cooperate with him. I entered the office of Dr. Vesna Bosanac where I found another person, another man. I wanted to talk to Dr. Vesna Bosanac tete-a-tete about the information that I had learned in the corridor, and I asked this man to leave the office. Before that, I forgot to say, when I arrived at the gate, when I was introduced -- when the -- sorry, when the commanders of the units told me what the situation in the hospital was like and what one could see there, I also asked that my assistant commander for counter-intelligence work, Mladen Karan, be called to come there. And now when I was entering for the second time this office, he appeared at the door. Mrs. Vesna Bosanac said to me, "It's not just anybody, it's Mr. Marin Vidic, Bili, the commissioner of the Croatian government for the town of Vukovar, and he should remain in the office." I agreed with her. We had a brief talk there and I asked her, or rather, I asked whether Dr. Gordana Antic is there and she said that yes, she was there, and I asked her to have her called in. She called one of her employees and asked her to find her. I said that they should take the medicine. And in Vesna Bosanac's office, I left my assistant commander and Mr. Borsinger stayed there as well. I went further on. Vesna Bosanac followed me. I told her that it wasn't necessary for her to accompany me because I would go with Major Paunovic, so she went back from this entrance into the hospital. We went out through the different entrance. When you go right from her office and then straight ahead, I think that's the main entrance. Paunovic took me to see that shelter where the headquarters had been of the National Guards Corps. I could just see it from the outside because we noticed that the shelter had been mined and that there were quite a few booby-traps. I remembered that the entrance was between two make-shift buildings. It was made of concrete. And in front there was an armoured Mercedes that was a bit damaged, but what remains striking in my memory is that it had foreign licence plates. I think they were German but I cannot be sure of that. I said to Paunovic that they should be increasingly alert, that soldiers should not touch this, and that they should not enter the shelter until the engineering units come in and demine it. So we did not take anything or see anything except from the outside, and then we returned to the hospital once again. Again, I talked to Dr. Bosanac. I asked her about lists of wounded, injured persons. She showed me some papers that she got out of the drawer. They were quite messy. There were some names on the lists and then there weren't any on others, and so on. She explained that it was difficult, in a situation of war and in the situation that they were in, to keep all papers in proper order. I told my assistant commander for counter-intelligence to check all these papers, to check these lists, and to see whether we can find out who is in the hospital and how many wounded there are. Then Dr. Antic arrived. I had wished to talk to her in Vesna's office. She asked me to go outside to conduct this conversation. I went out in front of the hospital with her, we were on our own, and we talked. She also said that she wanted to help and do whatever she could. I told her that I was called by the general and that he asked me to get her to Sid during the night. She asked me whether I could make it possible for her to go straight to Hungary rather than Sid. I told her that I really didn't have the authority to do that, and I told her the only thing I could do was have her transported to Sid. She thought about it a bit and she said that that evening she did not want to leave, and that in the morning she would decide what she would do afterwards. I went along with her wish. After that, I returned -- or rather, I don't know whether I went back to the office, but I found Major Paunovic there. Mr. Borsinger went out. And it was almost dark by then. I made an offer to Mr. Borsinger. I asked him whether he wanted to come with me and see these corpses that the commanders had told me about, and what he told -- what he said to me, roughly, as far as I can remember, was that he was in a hurry; that he had seen everything he was interested in in the hospital and that he had to arrive in Belgrade, I don't know, that he had some engagements there and that he could not go and see that with me then. He asked me when the evacuation of the hospital would start. I said to him that that would probably start on the following day, at daybreak, immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a question. On that day, were you informed, or was anybody else informed, that Mr. Borsinger had any objections to the way the army was behaving that day in the hospital; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've already given an answer but I wanted to be precise. Did Borsinger object to anything regarding this proposal and agreement that the civilians should go to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not object. As a matter of fact, he suggested that the hospital be emptied and that the civilians go, so they would be evacuated as soon as possible, because their people were on the ground all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that afternoon, and then we're going to talk about the next day, did Borsinger ever mention to you the concept of neutrality of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about that and I did not talk about that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that afternoon, evening or night, at any point in time did you come to the hospital again?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the evening, when I went back, I did not go back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Borsinger ask you or did you hear him ask from anyone -- ask anyone else that they remain in the hospital that night?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not ask for that. As a matter of fact, he asked to leave because he said he had other engagements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me see whether there are any interventions or any suggestions. Would you just be as precise as possible. What did Borsinger say to you about Velepromet? Were his teams there or not? Can you be more precise about that.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borsinger suggested to Vesna Bosanac, Mrs. Vesna Bosanac, that civilians should go to Velepromet because that is where their teams were. And they were there on the first day and on that day and they were following the evacuation of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see what happened after you left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went with Major Paunovic and I saw many corpses in that street where he pointed them out to me. I found it very hard to see that. It was almost nightfall by then. I went back. I called my assistant, Karan. He told me that he had taken some papers, some lists, the ones that I told him about, but he also told me that he saw that Mrs. Vesna Bosanac had given some lists to Mr. Borsinger that were far tidier than the ones that we had had. I said, "All right, then. Fine." I don't know whether he had found any other material there. I cannot recall all the details right now. I asked Mr. Paunovic, the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the military police, to bring to Negoslavci Mrs. Vesna Bosanac and Mr. Marin Vidic so that we could have a talk. Then I returned to Negoslavci with my vehicle and I was waiting -- or rather, first I went to see the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Now I'm just going to put a few things to you that you had heard yourself in this courtroom. On page 683 of the transcript of the 27th of October, Mrs. Bosanac says that, on that day, you came to the hospital twice and that you came with Borsinger during the night. Just tell us, without a comment, yes or no; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I told you in detail, I made an effort to tell you all the things that I did in the hospital at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please not speak at the same time at the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 1021, on transcript page from the 11th of October -- November. 1521. I do apologise to the interpreters. Mr. Njavro testified that he saw you on the 18th of November, around 1300 hours, with Mr. Borsinger in front of the hospital; is that correct? Were you by the hospital on that day?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is sheer nonsense. There are video recordings as to where I was on the 18th of November. I first came to the hospital on the afternoon of the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A few witnesses, P22 and P009, mention that on that afternoon, when they came to the area in front of the hospital, they saw quite a few local people gathered there and who were threatening and who said that these people should be killed. With regard to that testimony and with regard to your own recollections, on that day, when you were at the hospital, in front of the hospital, did you hear such comments, and were you informed about that, that there were serious threats that were being issued to people who were in the hospital, or any kind of threats, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the hospital yard and further on, where I was moving about, I did not hear any threats or anything that would be something that I would consider to be a lack of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness Cakalic, when he testified on the 13th of March, transcript page 59 -- 5893, said that in the night between the 18th and the 19th, or rather, at dawn, you personally took Marin Vidic out of the hospital; that you were in the office and that then you took him out.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite incorrect. I said where I found Marin Vidic. Mr. Paunovic will come here to testify. And I gave him the task of bringing Marin Vidic in and he did bring him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, and I'm going to put something that you heard in this courtroom to you. I found that to be important; maybe the Prosecution is going to put other things to you. Mr. Njavro, also on the 11th of November, when he testified, transcript page 1535, when he described a dialogue he had with a person he called Radic, he said that this person said to him that you had told him to mistreat people. Did you tell anyone, any officer, any soldier, to mistreat anyone in the hospital during the course of that night or at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is wholly untrue. It would be a shame for me to behave that way. I would have been ashamed of any such thing. I was chief of security, as you said. I had a certain authority; I was at a certain level. I did my best to do my work properly and I trusted that people who were supposed to carry out the tasks that were given to them. As for Captain Radic, I watched him as I did other commanders, komandiri, but after reaching Milovo Brdo, I do not recall having seen him anywhere and I did not issue any tasks to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about somebody else?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from anyone on that day, that night, that evening, or the following day, that European monitors or anyone else wanted to go to the hospital that night?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that except for here. I think that somebody talked about something like that in the courtroom. But all who came to our zone were made aware of the curfew from 1700 hours until 6.00 in the morning, and that then, almost no one was moving around in the zone unless there was some exceptional need to save a life or to help people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After coming from the hospital, again, I reported to the command, to the commander, and I reported to him that we took the medicine there. I said to General Panic that Dr. Antic did not want to go to Sid. Then I told Commander Mrksic about what I had found there and I informed him that I had asked for Vesna Bosanac to be called in for an interview with me and Marin Vidic as well. And probably we talked about other things, too, but I cannot remember everything. I remember that after that, Mr. Mrksic said the following to me: that I should no longer ask for vehicles from the European Red Cross for evacuating the hospital because all of this had been regulated, and that on the following morning the evacuation of the hospital would start; that officers and vehicles would come from the 1st Military District and that Colonel Pavkovic was in charge of that effort. He gave me the following task: that I must ensure full security to have all of those who are suspected of having committed war crimes taken out of the hospital first so that they would be transported to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica. As for the transport of these persons, I should report to the assistant for logistics; that he had already been ordered to assign buses for that. That before going to the hospital, I should report to the head of the medical service, Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic, and that Mr. Mrksic had already given him the task to assign ten military doctors who should examine the wounded together with the doctors of the Vukovar Hospital, and that security organs, during the screening, are not allowed to take anyone out of the hospital without having these persons first having been examined by doctors and in their presence, that I should not carry out any kind of triage without the doctors being with me, the doctors who had been assigned to that task. I accepted that and we scheduled this for 6.00 the following morning. I was off to organise my own business and to interview Vesna Bosanac and Marin Vidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think I will be addressing all the counts in the indictment, just some that we'll not be addressing now. The Prosecutor says that Commander Mrksic conferred upon you the power to conduct an evacuation, which the OTP claims started at the hospital, went through the barracks, and ended up at Ovcara. The Prosecutor also claims that you commanded all the forces that were involved in this evacuation from the hospital to Ovcara. Please tell us if that is true.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is entirely erroneous. I never received an order like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can have a look now at what you did after the meeting at Colonel Mrksic's.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to that building, near where I drew the command post of the town commander. The forensics were there already; my two security clerks and Vesna Bosanac as well. I talked to her briefly. Most of all, I wanted to see if she could help me find the commander, Mr. Jastreb. I wanted to know about the numbers of the wounded and who the remaining people in the hospital were. She said she was willing to help. She said there were plenty of people there and she didn't know the exact figure. But if I remember correctly the figures she gave me at the time, although they may be inaccurate, she said, I believe, that there were over 200 wounded and about 60 inpatients. But I wasn't very familiar with some of the more medical/technical terms that she was using. And then she said, "Sir, the only ones to remain faithful to their people until the bitter end are myself," and she meant herself, "and Mr. Marin Vidic. And you will not find this gentleman you're after because he has long fled Vukovar." I asked her again but she said, "I'm sorry, I can't help you." I wanted to see if I could do anything about her being taken to Zagreb, or rather, she asked me and I said I would do everything within my power. I asked her whether she was in touch with anyone in Zagreb. She said she was permanently in touch with Mr. Tus and she could always call him any time she wanted. The same with Mr. Hebrang and Mr. Tudjman. I told her that I would find the names of some officers who I knew had been taken prisoner in other JNA barracks, in Croatia, in Gospic, and other parts of Croatia. I'm not mentioning other names, just to avoid hurting that person's feelings. I was looking for a major who had served with me in the Guards Brigade but who had then been transferred to the Gospic barracks. It was the previous spring that he was captured and nobody knew what had become of him. I was adamant that I should find out about this man's fate and she promised to give me a hand with this. Just after our conversation --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac started talking about politics, about Tudjman, how he had betrayed them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please kindly be asked to speak one at a time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The messenger came to see me to call me back to the commander's post. I came and Mr. Mrksic was seated at a table in the operations room. There were three other high-ranking officers, colonels, seated at the same table as well as a number of other officers. I think this was about 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You saw that entrance -- that entry in the war log about that. I will not be showing this now. This was at about 2000 hours. Was that the thing that jogged your memory?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, but the log was also discussed. It said 7.30, possibly 8.00, and then the log was in that building where we interviewed Vesna Bosanac. We were watching TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So tell us what happens now.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The colonel briefly addressed me to say, "These are officers from the security administration. They're here on a mission. Their mission is to conduct a triage and to identify any crime suspects so that they might then be taken to Sremska Mitrovica. Please sit down with them and tell them about the security situation in the area of responsibility of the Guards Brigade." I greeted those men. I had never met any of those officers before; didn't know a single one of them. I started my briefing. I told them that in the area covered by our brigade, those who had surrendered had already been evacuated, as well as anyone from the Mitnica area, and there was no one left there now. The only two places where there were still men to be screened were Velepromet and the hospital. I said that Velepromet was under the control of the Vukovar TO and that that was the place where a screening was needed the most. I made a proposal and Colonel Mrksic reacted right away that the hospital was not to be touched until the following morning. I was interrupted immediately by the leader of that group. He introduced himself as Bogdan Vujic, Colonel Bogdan Vujic. And this is roughly what he said to me: "Major, Comrade, we know all of that but we must get on. And this is what we'll do. My team," that is, the team that arrived with Bogdan Vujic, "will go straight to Velepromet to do some work there. You assign an officer to us who will introduce us to the people there. You carry on interviewing the persons that you have been interviewing and also prepare for the triage and the selection process at the hospital. But you can't go to the hospital before you've talked to me," since this had already been scheduled for 6.00 the following morning. "Tomorrow morning report to me at the Velepromet gate with the team at 6.00 sharp," he said. The commander had already issued an assignment to the duty operations officer to use the military police battalion to provide escort for those people as far as Velepromet. I phoned the barracks to speak to my security assistant, Srecko Borisavljevic. I told him to meet these officers at the Velepromet gate and to introduce them to the representatives of the Territorial Defence and the Velepromet warden so that -- and that he should be with them until they carried out all their assignments, and this is where we parted ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hold on a second, please. You've heard the evidence of Mr. Vujic on the 16th of February. On page 4497, he said that. As they were setting off, you said this: "Don't be surprised if you see a Chetnik slit the throat of an Ustasha there."

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read different statements made by this gentleman, Mr. Vujic, when I arrived in The Hague, since they became available at the time. One thing I realised is that he tends to change his statements very often. I'm not repeating what you've already said. He added something on his way into the courtroom also what the purpose was behind him -- behind him making these additions to his statement. I don't know. But all these things are lies, pure lies. He even said that I had held a meeting outside the headquarters. Your Honours, our army was a serious army. I don't even wish to go into statements of that kind. It is up to you to judge what is right and what is wrong, but it would have been a little too much for a major to be lining up colonels for review and to be giving them orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's not go any further into that. You never said any such thing, based on what I gather from the conversation between the two of you.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never stated any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at any point throughout that evening meet those persons again?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the same evening. It wasn't before the next morning, at 6.00, when I reported to Colonel Vujic at the Velepromet gate, that I saw them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to something different now, but before we do, I wish to put something else to you. I would like to stay in public session. I can tell you the name, if you like, but then we'll have to go into private session. Witness P32, testifying on the 7th of December - 6962 is the reference in the transcript - he claims he saw you on the 19th, the morning of the 19th, in the hospital area. You put him in the vehicle you were using, he says, and then drove him to the hospital. Do you remember this witness and what he said?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the evidence but, believe me, it's very difficult to keep track of all these codes, P0, P3. Where I live, we use last names, not codes. Be that as it may, his evidence is simply not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will be asking you some questions about the Velepromet facility now. Can you tell us whose facility it was? Who was there? Who was securing the facility? Who was holding the facility? Was it someone from your own security organs? Did they go there? Were they there, and what did they do? Generally speaking, a word or two about Velepromet, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velepromet is a huge warehouse of some sort of a wholesaler or trading company or something, or that's what it used to be in peacetime. By the time we got there, a holding centre had been set up there for Vukovar's residents. It was the Vukovar TO that controlled this facility. They had their own food storage there, fuel and ammunition. They had special rooms to hold people who needed putting up. They knew the people. And we didn't interfere very much but we tried to help as much as we could. For the most part, it was their men securing Velepromet. For members of the Guards Brigade, Velepromet was not very important, or at least not before the 18th of November. We hardly ever went there. However, the commander of the 2nd Assault Detachment had been given the task of making sure there was sufficient order and discipline there, and you can see that based on the order that was issued by Colonel Mrksic. I personally gave Captain Srecko Borisavljevic a task, and that was pursuant to the commander's order. There is an entry to show that in the war log. I gave him the task of occasionally controlling the security situation in the holding centre and to work with the security organs. In this case, the man was called Zigic, the TO security person. And I also told him to exchange any useful information with Zigic. So much about Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you know about whoever was in charge of the centre?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubinko Stojanovic was in charge of the holding centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he was ...

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the TO. And based on my information and based on what Srecko Borisavljevic had told me, he was a hard-working, capable fellow and he did his job really well. The ICRC men and the European monitors often came to talk to him, and Mr. Vance also went to talk to him when he was visiting Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just something about the transcript. It's page 23, line 25, "Ljubinko Stojanovic" is the name. And page 24, line 2, he was not the commander of the TO; he was a member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a member of the Vukovar TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had you ever heard anything about any irregularities, crimes being committed, in Velepromet prior to this period?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd heard no such thing throughout my time in Vukovar, nothing to indicate that there had been anything like that at all in Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to use the e-court system now to look at the war log. This is Exhibit 70. The B/C/S -- 107, my apologies. The war log, it's 107. The B/C/S page is 33, and the e-court reference is 02935466. The English is page 30. My apologies, it's 401. The exhibit number is 401. It's the war log of the Guards Brigade. We all know it by heart, I believe, or perhaps we don't. 401. The B/C/S page is 33 and the English is page 30. The entry is dated the 22nd. 02935466. The last bit, if you can, please, if you can blow it up a little, it's the last entry on this page. It's dated the 22nd of October, 1330 hours. I'll read it out. "The commander of OG South ordered that in the Velepromet company where refugees are being gathered, there should always have been one security officer to gather information," and then I think what it says in parentheses is "(chief of security)."

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've talked about this already even before you read this out. I told you that I had put Captain Srecko Borisavljevic in charge of this task and he was also a security clerk in the 2nd Assault Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at another two documents from our 62 ter batch, which also referred to Velepromet which is why I left them for this stage in the proceedings. Can we now put on the screen 65 ter, 13 documents marked 3D050058. That is 3D050058. That is again a report of the security organ of the Guards Brigade from November the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I should like to deal first with the second paragraph, Mr. Sljivancanin, and hear your comments. "In the 1st Battalion of the military police," that is how it starts. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also a report of mine addressed to the chief of security in the cabinet of the Federal Secretary. While I can read out for you what is written in it, this was a practice -- this refers to 26 Croatian soldiers from the 1st Battalion of the military police who started to worry about their future fate because they had learned that the Republic of Croatia had proclaimed, on the 10th of November, that it would be independent, and it was only normal that people should be concerned. This is what I wrote about in these reports of mine, seeking advice as to allow a further course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph speaks for itself. It confirms that on that day there were also those problems that we talked about yesterday in the anti-terrorist company. But what I should like to deal with now is the last paragraph on the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we turn the page, please, over. Can we zoom in on the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is what it says: "By the liberation of the settlement Bosko Buha in Vukovar, after that, rather, suddenly emerged -- appeared a large number of people in the shelters. Over 300 persons were evacuated to Velepromet where they were individually processed. During the day, around 100 persons were processed, from which number around 25 persons were singled out as being of relevance to the security organs in terms of the further gathering of data on the positions and forces of the Ustasha units and for the possible exchange for captured JNA members," and then you go on to explain who was in question. Can you give us a brief comment on this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is written here is true. That is the way it was at that time. We, the security organs, could suspect people of having committed a crime only if we caught them red-handed, on the spot, on the crime scene, or if they surrendered with weapons or if we caught them in the act. As regards other persons, they had to be processed. They had to be subjected to the selection process in which we were assisted by members of the Territorial Defence of Vukovar, also on the basis of the list that we received from the security administration on the identification of such persons. We then processed such persons and then decided whether they were civilians or should be detained. There were 25 such people, and if I remember correctly, as I said yesterday, it was proved that only two or three had committed certain criminal offences. The others were let go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document -- but before we do that, I should like to ask that we move into private session. Can we just have a mark given to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be marked for identification, if that's what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to mark it for admission into the case file, into the evidence, and I was referring to the next document when I asked for us to go into private session because it refers to the name of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you're tendering this document, it will be received, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 834, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. This document will become Exhibit 835, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we shall manage to deal with another topic before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Ovcara that evening, Mr. Sljivancanin? We are still talking about the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, after my meeting with organs from the security administration, I remained at the command post, because officers were coming, having accomplished certain tasks, and information was coming in. And I, of course, was interested in hearing the information and seeing what was going on. And as far as I can remember, Major Skoric was also among the people returning. Major Skoric had been assigned the night before to lead civilians to Croatia, to the highway, to the crossing at Sid. And he reported that Croatia did not want to take in those people, and as far as I could learn, they were returned to Ovcara again. That was a big problem for the people concerned, and I remember the words uttered, which were, "Why is it allowed for those people to be maltreated?" I think that they also, in passing, talked to the chief of the quartermaster service who was supplying food and water for those people and he adduced a series of problems. He even said that Territorial Defence members were there and that they were cannibalising certain vehicles - that is what he said - because he had just returned from the region of Ovcara. So these were all the problems that were being conveyed to me, and I was a bit taken aback. I wasn't aware that all this was happening. And I feel sorry for those people because the night before I had worked on those things with Major Vukasinovic. I don't know whether Colonel Mrksic said something about that to me. I might have talked about it with him also, but I am not quite sure. I cannot remember. So I went and called Major Vukasinovic and he and I went to Ovcara directly. I couldn't go on my own because of security considerations and it was dark. As we were approaching Ovcara, we were stopped at a gate which was installed by the command post there. For at least 20 minutes they wouldn't let us enter, because the curfew was on and they didn't know us and we didn't know them because they were from another unit. After some insistence, this commander from that command post actually made an appearance or called in and he checked and verified who we were. He let us in. And with our vehicle, we came outside the so-called yellow building. There, an officer of rank of captain first class, in uniform - I remember that - told me that there were a large number of civilians who had returned, that they would not disembark from the buses to be placed in the hangar, that they wanted to stay on the buses, that they had ensured water and food for them; but he said that everything was all right and that the military police had arrived to secure that -- the place. And, according to him, there were no problems whatsoever. There, I also found the commander, one of the komandiri of the Territorial Defence, Miroljub Vujevic, accompanied by several members of the Territorial Defence. I asked him what business he had being there and he told me that he had come on account of the motor vehicles and the mechanisation, the machines that were supposed to come to Velepromet that had been extracted from Mitnica but had not yet arrived; not all of the machinery had arrived. Of course, as it was dark, I didn't go out to check. There was no lighting or anything there. I told him that he should rest assured that the members of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army would not take or take away anything that belonged to anybody else; that that would be put in Velepromet; that he should wait for daybreak -- for day and that that would be solved. So this officer said what his name was but I forgot. He was a representative of the 80th Motorised Brigade. He said that there were no problems, that it would be regulated according to the orders received. And he offered me to go and see those people on the buses. I thought that it was not necessary for us to go and see those people that we -- I cannot say ill-treated, but we only helped, in fact, last night; that there was no need to expose them to any further such treatment, and that actually -- that was not the task of my unit. So we stayed there for about 10 or 15 minutes and then we went back. Vukasinovic went to his own building; I went to my command post. As far as I can recall, I believe that I told Colonel Mrksic that I had been at Ovcara, although I'm not 100 per cent sure of that, and I believe that he said to me, "Well, I know all of that. Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic, the commander of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear of what.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of the 80th Brigade has informed me about all of that. And that evening I met for the first time with General Aca Vasiljevic and Colonel Tumanov.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. You have to repeat the previous sentence. What did Colonel Mrksic tell you when you reported to him upon returning from Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just slow down. What did Mrksic tell you that had been told to him?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember that, I talked to Mrksic that time. More or less, this is what Mrksic told me. He told me that he knew that the people had been returned to Ovcara, that he had been informed about that by Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic, the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and that all the necessary measures to take proper care of those people had been taken and that he knew that there were no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 32, line 12, the witness said "Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic." We shall continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They stand to the left and they stand to the right. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I possibly ask one small indulgence from my learned friend. I know how difficult it is when one is taking a witness in chief, especially one like Mr. Sljivancanin who is important, but sometimes the questions will have two or three questions in the question; more importantly, the answers are enormously long. And I, for my part, would be extremely grateful - perhaps it's my inability to take so much material in quickly - but I would be very grateful if, in actual fact, my learned friend could control Mr. Sljivancanin, as best he can, so that the answers become intelligible. They may require cross-examination in due course. And it is not a criticism, just merely a request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in relation to my planned sequence of questions and current questions, I have full control of the witness. Possibly his answers are a bit long, but that's because we carried out intensive preparations, the two of us. And sometimes, in response to some of my questions, he gives me three or four answers to three or four possibly questions. If Mr. Moore does not find some of these things clear, perhaps we will be able to clarify them, as we did yesterday, but he will have plenty of time during the cross-examination. What I am doing is making an effort to take Mr. Sljivancanin through a great many topics as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we will try, first and foremost, for the efficiency of these proceedings, to be as clear as possible, Mr. Sljivancanin, and we would like the answers to be what we can proffer to the Court. Mr. Sljivancanin, we broke off when you went back to Mrksic. Who did you find there at Mr. Mrksic's when you arrived back from Ovcara on the 19th, in the evening? And what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already started saying, I found General -- Major General Aca Vasiljevic there, then Colonel Tumanov, and there were other officers there from the 1st Military District, then from the General Staff, too. But I cannot remember their names, and I didn't even know some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Tumanov? Who was he then?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time he was the deputy of Aca Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I briefly informed General Vasiljevic and Tumanov about what we security organs did over the previous two days, especially in Mitnica. When a group of officers came and -- from the security administration, I said that they went to Velepromet. And I said that I brought in Dr. Vesna Bosanac and Marin Vidic for an interview and that I asked them to come to the same premises where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your view, did Vasiljevic respond to you? Did he know anything about the group from the security administration that came? Was that referred to?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was referred to. He said that he knew and, as a matter of fact, he even advised me, or rather, he suggested to me that these are experienced officers and that, in my future work, as far as security matters are concerned, I should cooperate with them and that I should go by the instructions that they give me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go after that? What happened?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I went to my building and -- well, I forgot something here. I don't remember now whether I sent Mrs. Vesna Bosanac to go to sleep before or after I went to Ovcara. I cannot remember all these details. But, at any rate, I told her, since it was night-time and there was a curfew on, that it was risky to travel to the hospital at night; that nearby we had a hospital of our own and that quite a few nurses and lady doctors were there, because I didn't want her, as a female person, to spend the night at the buildings where we were spending the night. So I was suggesting to her that she spend the night in our hospital and to see how our doctors worked and to see who they were treating. She agreed to that. I called Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic and I asked that he receive the doctor at the hospital and provide whatever was necessary for her. We did not apply any kind of measures of coercion vis-a-vis her, except for the fact that I said to her that on the next day, at 6.00 in the morning, she would go to the hospital together with me and that we would continue our conversation. Then I continued talking to Mr. Marin Vidic, Bili.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where was this conversation taking place, and do you remember who was present there? And at what time this happened in the evening, can you tell us, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Marin Vidic, Bili, in the evening, sometime before midnight, on the 19th of November, 1991, in the premises of the building where the security organ was. I made a drawing of this here. Karan was present, Borce Karanfilov, and perhaps some of the crime scene technicians who were recording these interviews on camera. I cannot remember the names of all of these persons, but the two I mentioned were there for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anybody come during this interview? Did anybody enter your rooms?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, around 12.00 at night, or rather, at midnight or perhaps a bit later, General Vasiljevic came and Colonel Tumanov.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us repeat once again: Where was this taking place?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was taking place in the premises of the house where the security organs were staying in the village of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was it that was happening there? What were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked General Vasiljevic that perhaps he talk to Mr. Vidic as well. The general said that he did not want to conduct any conversations with him, that I should take care of it. He also asked me that I should show him all the documents I had, that I managed to collect from members of the National Guards Corps and that I managed to find until then, in the course of our work, and also what we took away from the volunteers that we were disarming and sending outside the zone of combat. He was asking questions about the method of work that we were carrying out then. We briefly discussed the telegram as well that I had received from him. I said to him, "We are doing whatever we can with regard to this matter." He suggested to me that, without any interviews, we should send all suspects to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica and that there were organs there that would further investigate these persons. These were the brief conversations that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This building where your rooms were, if I can put it that way, the ones that you showed us on the first day, is that the building where you slept otherwise, where you - how should I put this? - spent time when you were not outside?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the building where we slept, where we stayed, when we were not out in the field, and we spent our time only in that building during the time of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who else slept in that building along with you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karan, Karanfilov, Momcilovic. For a while, before he became commander of this place, Vukasinovic slept there, too. And my driver did as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that evening, did you go out after this conversation with Vidic, after Mr. Vasiljevic came? Did you leave the building during the course of the night?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very tired because I hadn't slept the previous night, and I could hardly wait for this activity of ours to be over, to get a bit of rest, knowing of the exertion that lay ahead. I didn't go anywhere. I continued talking to Mr. Marin Vidic, who handed over his diary to me and quite a few other papers that he had written to the President of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Tudjman. Once he said that previously he had been a musician and that he liked nightlife. And he asked me if I had a glass of brandy for him and I said that I was not really a drinker. But then I asked for a drink to be brought for him and they brought him a glass. And we sang. He sang well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you give any tasks out for the following day to your people?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening I gave assignments for the next day. As for Major Vukasinovic, I said that he should get two buses that would go to the area of the hospital and transport suspects, crime suspects, who were hiding at the hospital. As for Captain Karan, I assigned him to get the documents from the hospital and to go to the hospital together with me and Dr. Bosanac. As for Captain Karanfilov, I assigned him to continue talks with Marin Vidic in the morning, and that he should go to the shelter that should be demined so that we see what was in that shelter where the headquarters of the ZNG had been. At the same time I asked an officer from the engineering unit to assign some professionals to remove the booby-traps so that the security organs could enter the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we move on to the 20th of November, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, there is one thing that I didn't say about the 19th. There is such a lot of information. That evening, on orders from Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic, a doctor, lieutenant colonel, called me, Lieutenant Colonel Ivezic, and he told me that he was assigned to take the doctors to the Vukovar Hospital. And the lieutenant colonel told him to report to me and that I would tell him what to do. And I said to him that in the morning, at 6.00, we would go to the Vukovar Hospital; that they were supposed to carry out their tasks there and that we agree on the spot, but they should be ready to leave with us at 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So did you actually leave at 6.00 in the morning? Who left? Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We assembled, perhaps just before 6.00. There were my driver and I in this vehicle; Captain Karan was there and Dr. Ivezic. In the other vehicle, there was, I think, Vesna Bosanac. And whether there was another vehicle driving behind that vehicle, I think there were doctors driving in that one that Captain Ivezic had brought along. We set out on the morning of the 20th, and we met Colonel Bogdan Vujic at the Velepromet gate in Vukovar at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happens next?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to Colonel Vujic; I told him the team was there. He asked how many seats were available in my car and I said there was one seat available, but no room left. He said, "We ought to find room for another officer." I said, "If the man doesn't mind, he can have a seat in the trunk of the car," because there was still room there. They said, "All right." We talked briefly about where those suspects should be taken. Earlier on there had been a plan for all civilians - we took them all to be civilians simply because these people had surrendered unarmed; it wasn't like we caught them in the act, committing a crime - they were all to go through Velepromet first. We, the security organs, were to be there for the screening and we didn't believe that those people should be sent back to Velepromet to be searched, to be screened, if you like; rather, we agreed that the best course of action would be for them to be taken to the barracks, for them to wait there until a convoy was formed to go to Sremska Mitrovica. The colonel gave some other assignments to those other officers, his own officers who were there, but that's not something I concerned myself with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So who came with you in that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Bogdan Vujic and another officer from the security organ, but, believe me, at the time I didn't know his name, and I still don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But now you know who he was, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I do. As I was preparing for all of this, I learnt that this was Korica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The previous day you talked to Colonel Mrksic about the hospital evacuation and your assignment. What was the plan? What did Mrksic tell you? What did you learn? Where were all those persons to be taken to, the persons who were crime suspects, potential perpetrators of crimes?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the 18th of November, at that meeting, Mrksic said that all crime suspects, or all those who had surrendered as crime suspects, were to be taken to Sremska Mitrovica, to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica, whereas the civilians could be taken to two different places - either to the Red Cross headquarters in Sid or to a place along the Croatian border where it was agreed that they would be received. There were also those who wanted to remain in Vukovar and it was said that those people should be allowed to do so undisturbed and unharassed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Prior to the 20th - do you perhaps know this? - had anyone mentioned that anyone was to be taken to Ovcara on the 20th of November from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was concerned, the entire area of the town of Vukovar bordering on the Velepromet area, there was the instruction that only civilians should go to Velepromet and no one from that area ever said anything about anyone being taken to Ovcara, nor was that necessary. The only thing was that Mitnica, as a Vukovar neighbourhood, a part of Mitnica bordered on the general Ovcara area, and in order to continue on to Sremska Mitrovica, some of those persons were sent through that facility in order to continue their journey from there on to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the hospital? Did it, in your words, gravitate more towards Velepromet or towards Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That facility gravitated towards Velepromet and the barracks alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were off to the hospital, I suppose. Tell me something else: Outside Velepromet at that point, on the 20th, or on the way to the hospital, as you talked to Vujic and the other people, did anyone at this time tell you about what had occurred at Velepromet the previous night? Did they share any of their impressions with you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officer who drove with us kept silent, for the most part. Myself, Dr. Vujic and Dr. Ivezic did most of the talking. Nothing at all was said about what they had done at Velepromet, nor was he, in any way, required to brief me on any of that. For the most part, we talked with Dr. Ivezic was about what the best way was to avoid hurting anyone, to avoid any disruptions to the life of the wounded, whatever that meant. Another important thing was to establish if there were any potential crime suspects there and how to screen the men, and that's what we discussed on our way to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you find, as far as officers from the Guards Brigade were concerned, upon your arrival at the hospital? Which soldiers were there, which military officers? Anyone from the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we reached the hospital that morning, there were soldiers and officers there from the 2nd Military Police Battalion. As far as I remember, Major Paunovic, Radoje Paunovic, was there and Captain Simic. I am certain about the two of them. There were other officers from the military police, but I can't quite remember who. I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard evidence by certain witnesses about what happened that night at the hospital, the night between the 19th and the 20th. Did those officers there tell you about any incidents at the hospital the previous night?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked Mr. Major Paunovic whether the night had been a quiet one. He didn't tell me about anything bad happening at the hospital, nor did he make any negative observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happens next?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to Mrs. Bosanac's office. We asked Mrs. Vesna Bosanac to summon her doctors who were supposed to be working together with our military physicians in order to inspect the hospital patients and the wounded. Dr. Ivezic did most of the talking as to how this was to be carried out. Bogdan Vujic left me there to deal with that. He said that he would be off with Officer Korica to pursue their own plans. After a brief discussion, Mrs. Vesna Bosanac came up with the idea that it would be best to have a meeting with all the medical staff attending so that our doctors could introduce themselves to their doctors and so that they could explain what needed doing. And she was willing to help us with this. I asked her how much time it would take for her to get everyone assembled. She said, "Ten minutes will do." And she also proposed a room where all these people would assemble. And, indeed, she convened some of her lady associates and then they told us to go to that room where the hospital staff had already assembled. Vesna Bosanac, Dr. Ivezic and I reached the room together. When you leave Bosanac's office, this room was just on the right-hand side of the corridor and then left, towards the exit. I think they called it the plaster room, or at least that's how I heard them refer to it. Dr. Ivezic asked me to hold that meeting and to say whatever it was that I had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what did you say; do you remember? A word or two about that, please. What did you share with the medical staff?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a difficult time for words. All those people and we, together with them, had been through so much suffering over the previous period of time. I tried not to give a proper speech but, rather, to tell them what they really wanted to know, although I've heard all kinds of evidence here and many fabrications, to be sure. This is, in very rough terms, what I said: "Gentlemen, doctors, I'm here on behalf of the JNA." I'm not sure if I introduced myself or not. Perhaps I did; perhaps I didn't. "The JNA is here to help everyone in this town. We are one people. You doctors took the doctor's oath and you have no reason to fear anything at all. You, of all people, have no reason to fear. We don't want to know whose wounded you have been treating. The crux of the matter is you provided people with appropriate treatment and you did your job. It's a sad thing that this had to happen. It's a sad thing we started killing each other. I believe this will be a warning for everyone and I hope this will never happen again." I also said this: "I think Tudjman and the HDZ, most of everyone, are to blame for this." If I may just finish, please. I said: "I know you want to know what we are to do. There is a possibility that the JNA believes that all honourable and hard-working people, especially those in this hospital, especially those who want to carry on living in Vukovar, you should give us a hand, you should stay here and help us along. Those who do not wish to remain have three choices: Firstly, they can go to the Red Cross in Sid or else they can go to Croatia." I also pointed out that we had information to indicate that there were individuals hiding inside the hospital who were suspected of having committed crimes. Any such persons will be brought in for interviews. "It is in your best interest," I said, "to help us find these people." That is, in very rough terms, what I said at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you offer the medical staff and the doctors to carry on working at the hospital and to remain in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said already, I offered everyone a chance to stay because we needed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you tell them at the time, or anyone else, for that matter, that a new hospital director had been appointed, Dr. Ivezic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said at the time that until civilian control was reestablished, Dr. Ivezic will be in charge of the hospital. I introduced him, but I don't remember actually saying that he would be the hospital director. I said he would be in charge of all the hospital business.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at Exhibit 338, photograph number 23, for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this room, and do you recognise anyone in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. This is Lieutenant Colonel Ivezic, the doctor in uniform. There is the rank on his shoulder strap. That's him. And this room is probably the room where the doctor was checking the hospital patients and preparing them for the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We're done with this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the meeting in the plaster room, let me ask you a question. It's a question that stems from some allegations in the indictment. It's an agreed fact that you were there at that meeting in the plaster room. Mr. Sljivancanin, did you keep anyone in the meeting, hold people back from leaving the meeting, as the soldiers were going about their business taking away about 400 non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a lie and it's also sheer nonsense. All I wanted was to tell those people what was in store for them and to provide any assistance I could, without holding anybody back at all. I was at the meeting to begin with because Vesna Bosanac had asked me to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you several questions about the triage.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't tell you everything about the meeting yet. After my presentation, people spoke up because they had questions for me. The main questions were about where the civilians were to assemble who wanted to go to those two places. We hadn't quite organised ourselves yet, but at the meeting I said that any crime suspects would be taken outside the hospital and then to the left, the street; and those who were preparing to go to Sid or back to Croatia should head right of the entrance and should split up into two groups so that the column leaders or the convoy leaders would know. We didn't separate them off ourselves. They asked me what they were allowed to bring in terms of their belongings. I said we would be everything within our power to help them but there wouldn't be that much room in the vehicles, so the best thing was for them to bring the bare necessities and not really bring a lot of things, because I didn't know at the time how much room there would be in the vehicles, or how many vehicles, for that matter. They asked me whether families would be allowed to not be split up. I thought they met husband, wife, sons, daughters, that sort of thing. I said that had not -- had they not asked for it, we would have asked for it, we would have insisted on it, that we will not be splitting families up. But any crime suspects would have to go and be interviewed. And that was the end of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard the testimony of Zvezdana Polovina. You remember her words. She heard you say that the men would be taken to the barracks for brief interviews and that they would later be joining them. Do you remember saying anything like that at the meeting, since there were so many different things being said?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
