utterances.text: Whatever I told the civilians I tried not to upset them any more than they already were. I perhaps may have said that they would be taken for short interviews without saying that they would be taken to prison in Sremska Mitrovica in order to avoid creating any tensions, any anxiety in the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is triage? Who did the screening? Who participated in it, and how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the very word "triage" means the separation of people who are suspected of having committed a crime, and at that time, for us, they were -- these were primarily men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of what age?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the ages of 18 -- from the age of 18 and up, depending on the physical fitness, constitution, and the risk, and the existence of doubt. This screening was done by doctors, by security organs, and all of the people cooperating in the hospital, including some Territorial Defence members chosen to participate in that work and who knew the people. And, of course, military police soldiers also participated, if the doctors told them to take people out, or so. But I should like to stress that we received the most help in identifying such persons from the doctors of the Vukovar Hospital. I really didn't ask the doctors what ethnicity they were. Those who came forward themselves and offered assistance, they would assist us. Among others, Dr. Gjuro Njavro did so and he helped us in the screening process together with our doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. I should not like to be leading. If you stick to this, you referred to able-bodied men from the age of 18. Do you remember, according to regulations on national defence, what was the lowest age threshold for men able to serve in the army at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that young men who were 18 or over came to do their military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And recruitment, at what age was that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deal with recruitment, but as far as I can recall, it was from the age of 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I suppose that the screening took place of people who had traces to indicate that they were either sick people or wounded people. Were there any people who presented different appearances but, for you, were people that should be singled out, that should be in the group that should be singled out, according to your criteria for selection?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a case when Dr. Ivezic took one man -- brought one man to me, and he told me, "Let me show you what a wounded person looks like." His entire head was in bandages, and the doctor asked him, "What is your problem?" And he said he did not have a single eye. Then on the spot, the doctor, having probably learned that earlier from the doctors of the Vukovar Hospital, removed the bandage and this was a completely healthy possible. Well, now, there may have been -- there were probably other cases like this, but I didn't go to see what each soldier and what each doctor was doing because, of course, I had my own work to do. And if I didn't know, other persons would have been required. But I know that this was the case. And I did not hear here in this court that any person in the hospital, during the screening process, complained that anyone was taking -- exacting any reprisals in so doing against them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter could not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this meeting and after a short consultation with Mr. Njavro, for him to help our doctors, as he had promised the evening before, I went to Mrs. Vesna Bosanac's office and there we resumed our dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked to see whether we could establish contact with Zagreb and talk to the people and she said that she would enable us to do that. Then I -- she remained there with Mladen Karan and I went out -- while she was trying to establish that connection. And then I went out to the right side, to the area of the shelter -- where the shelter of the ZNG was. Members of the engineer units, demining units, arrived at the spot and I had a short consultation and agreement with them in order for them to clear the shelter of mines. They said that they could do so but that the area needed to be secured. The security had to be ensured, that no one could pass via the road from the Dunav Hotel towards the hospital until the shelter was demined, because it was in the immediate vicinity of the road. An armoured battalion unit was there in that area at the time, so I asked the captain to help me secure the area. And he informed me that morning that, in the immediate vicinity of the hospital, that evening, explosives had killed three soldiers from his own battalion, which, of course, touched me deeply as a human being. So I returned to the office of Vesna Bosanac in an organised fashion, and en route, in passing, I saw all these civilians who were flocking to go. I might have exchanged a word or two with some of them, but I cannot remember all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard testimonies here from two witnesses that said that you had said that the process should be expedited and that the process should not be allowed to drag on until nightfall. Do you remember that, having said something like that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not deny that perhaps in passing from the shelter to the hospital, through this group of civilians, I might have hurried them on. I may have said something to that effect. I cannot remember my every word. I do not deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why would it have been your objective for the process to be expedited?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective of expediting the process would have been in the fact that I knew that vehicles and a convoy were to arrive to take away the wounded at a scheduled time to a place called Zidine. We had a precise time schedule when they were to arrive at that point in order to be taken over by other organisations from Croatia, so we needed to create safe conditions for these wounded to set off on their journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, you, as the security organ, do you consider it safe for the evacuation of the wounded and the sick to start before a screening process has been conducted to check whether, in the hospital, there were any reasons which would jeopardise such an evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not safe. It is not safe, because at that time we had received information that around 2.000 armed members of the National Guards Corps and around 800 members of the MUP were fighting with weapons in Vukovar. To us surrendered only their members at Mitnica. By that time no one had surrendered from the hospital area, and we suspected - and that was later borne out to be true; and witnesses who will be coming here will probably confirm that - there were people with weapons hiding either in or around the hospital. And it was obvious that they could create problems in the evacuation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who searched those persons, and where were they taken? How did the searching process go, in a couple of words?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The search was probably -- not "probably," but it was done by the military police, the 2nd Battalion members, and, from the witness testimonies that I have heard here, this was just a routine search that was carried out in quite a correct fashion. I was, in fact, proud of the dignified and humane way in which these young people were treating all the persons. They were supposed to board the buses, under the guidance of Major Vukasinovic, to be led to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During this period of time, from the time when they were taken out - and we have heard testimonies also to that effect - so from the building of the hospital up to the time they boarded the buses and were taken to the barracks, did you leave the hospital compound?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember leaving the hospital compound during that time because I stayed on talking to Vesna Bosanac and talking to people from Zagreb by telephone from her office. And I also remained in the rooms of a doctor, a lady doctor, who offered to take me to her office and give me photographic material about everything that had been happening in the hospital during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we hear her name, or should we go to private session?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd prefer that we go into private session because I had promised that to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session for a minute, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of this second conversation with Vesna Bosanac, after the plaster room meeting, as it were, do you remember whether she talked to anyone and whether you talked to anyone?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked Vesna Bosanac -- actually, she pleaded with me, and I asked her to impart to us information obtained from the Croatian authorities in respect of a major taken prisoner in Gospic of whose fate nothing had been known for six months. And, to be brief, she just told me, "I will get in touch with," as she told me, "Mr. Tudjman, but I really think that we talk to Hebrang. I'm not sure." She said, "It will be better once I establish connection that I hand it over to you and you ask about the major's fate." And once she had got in touch with his secretary, male or female secretary, and after exchanging a few words with him and then with that gentleman, she told him, "A representative of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army is here in my office and he wants to talk to you." And she handed the receiver to me. So I took the receiver and I said who I was to the man, and I heard from the other side the words, "I do not wish to talk to a Chetnik." And he hung up and that was it. There was no more talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I rang up General Aca Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called him so as to consult with him because I had obtained a lot of information, both in the hospital -- to the effect that Dr. Njavro, too, was suspected of not having properly treated the patients and of having committed crimes. Many doctors also complained of the conduct of Dr. Vesna Bosanac, and it was then, for the first time, they reported a man who I later learned -- whose name I later learned was Anto Aric, and it was then, on the 20th, in the morning, that I saw him for the first time. He had come there in August on orders from Tudjman to discharge some tasks. And I consulted with General Vasiljevic in terms of what was I to do with these three people and about those three people, as well as with Mr. Marin Vidic. The general told me, "Here, Tumanov, let Tumanov explain what you are to do." Tumanov talked to me on the phone and, more or less, this is what he said: "Sljivancanin, you know the routine. You know the procedures. Send them to Sremska Mitrovica for interrogation." And that was the end of that conversation. After that I summoned to the command from the -- two escorts to be assigned from the 1st Battalion of the military police. Captain Bozic, Mile, came with a military police vehicle, and I entrusted my assistant, Mladen Karan, with the task of resolving the question of the departure of these people to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard the testimony of Vesna Bosanac here and she claimed that she had spent a very large part of that day in the barracks. Did you know anything about that at that time? Or do you know anything else related to her continued stay in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that here, but you will see from my further testimony how busy of a schedule of activities I had during the rest of that day. I'm sure that my assistant Karan did his job properly; I know that. But I really don't know where they stayed, whether they were held up anywhere. The man will come here and take the stand and will say that. But I do know for a fact that they were taken to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, when did these buses with these people who were separated, when did they leave the hospital? Did you see them off, or do you not remember exactly? What is that you know about this?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that after leaving the office of the mentioned doctor, I set out to the other bridge, if I can put it that way, on the Vuka River, where I was supposed to be met by a captain from whose unit some soldiers got killed, in order to find out how they got killed. And I know that I scheduled a meeting with him at 10.00; I remember that. That remains in my memory. And when I was leaving, going to that bridge, I saw that the buses were already moving away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see Exhibit 421 for a moment, please, the report of the Operations Group South of the 20th of November, at 1800 hours. If the last page can be displayed, please. I don't know whether it's 2 or 3. The lower part, if that can be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report from the 20th of November, at 1800 hours. Why is this document relevant in relation to what you have been testifying about just now?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably, we can see the names of the soldiers here. I even know the towns that these soldiers were from. One person was from Danilovgrad --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can say it. One was from Pozarevac; one was from Backa Palanka. The report is sent at 1800 hours, because the previous one was sent on the previous evening, on the 19th, at 1800 hours, and the soldiers were killed during the night between the 19th and the 20th. And they are all from the armoured battalion. These are the soldiers that I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Map 156, please. Could we just have that marked. If Mr. Sljivancanin can mark on that map [In English] evidence, Exhibit 156. [Interpretation] Could Mr. Sljivancanin use the pen to mark the place where this incident had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did these three soldiers get killed in the same incident, Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They got killed in the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be enlarged a bit, the part near the central part of the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can put a circle here, too, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Could the central part please be enlarged a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just mark it, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the area where they got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you describe it. Is it across the bridges? In relation to the bridges and the hospital, where is this?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is between the bridges on the Vuka and the hospital. It's closer to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we -- or rather, put number 1 there, Mr. Sljivancanin, and then let's have this admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 836, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, in the period before these buses had left and before this convoy came, the one that we are going to talk about now, did you see any trucks there or any ambulance vehicles at the time when the buses were there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard the dialogue that was described by Ljubisa Dosen, a witness here. Do you remember anyone who was taken out on a stretcher? Do you remember that dialogue, that story, and what she testified about with regard to her late husband?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry about all the things that the lady said and I am sorry about what happened to her husband. But also it is correct that many witnesses were just saying that they knew of Sljivancanin, that they didn't know any other officers there. There were quite a few officers there. But I really do not remember having talked to the mentioned lady at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there other officers there that were wearing camouflage uniforms like you at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same uniform and the same build, that's something that my assistant Vukasinovic had. And similar uniforms were worn by some other officers from the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the search within the compound, and as persons were boarding buses, were there any officers from the military police there? To the best of your recollection, do you remember how many officers were there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I saw Major Paunovic there and Captain Simic. I really do not remember who else I saw, but there should have been other platoon leaders there, at least three officers of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the trial, on the 3rd of November, on page 1160, Witness 006 testified. Probably you don't actually know who this is, so if necessary, we can move into private session. But he said that he, as a technical/medical man, was taken off the bus together with a few of his colleagues; that he was in front of the hospital, that he was put there; and that they waited there for about an hour; and that then you came and that you talked to him and returned him to the hospital. Has this jogged your memory? Do you remember that there was a group that was standing there and waiting there for a while until you talked to them?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you hear any statement, it either jogs your memory or you realise that that was not the case. I said that after I returned again to Vesna Bosanac's office, at one point in time, a lady came and said to me, "You promised that you would not separate families and our husbands were taken to the barracks." I asked, "How come?" She said, "Well, they're not there. They were taken away." I said, "Madam, make a list of all these husbands who you think are members of the hospital staff and that belong to your families. I promise you, if they had not committed any crimes, they will be with your families." The lady left, and after a certain amount of time - I don't know whether it was half an hour; more than that, less than that, I really don't know - at any rate, as I set out to see the places where these soldiers got killed, she brought me that list. I sent my driver to the barracks and I said to him that he should find Major Vukasinovic and that I asked that these persons from the list should be returned to the hospital. He went and took that list. Then, later, when I came with the representatives of the European Community and the Red Cross to the hospital, and with Colonel Pavkovic, I went towards the gate to see whether these persons, these men, had been returned. And I remember that I found a group of men there who were standing there. They said that they had been separated out there and that they had some kind of membership cards, as they had put it, of the hospital. I saw these passes that they had and I said that it was not necessary for them to stand there any longer. I said that they could go back and return to the hospital. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since a witness, another protected witness, said on page 3373 - the witness is 031 - on the 26th of January, said that you came to the bus, that he showed you his ID even before the buses left, that this ID did not have a photograph, and that you returned him to the bus. What do you say to that? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already answered that question. I was not present. I was not in the street when the buses left, so I could not have returned anyone on to the bus. But I know that I talked to people in the street who were waiting, allegedly, for transportation, and I found these people who had these IDs and I returned them to the hospital. As for the rest, I do not remember it -- well, there's nothing to remember. I never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A few moments ago, when you said that you agreed that the buses should go to the barracks, not to Velepromet, and that from there they would go further on to Sremska Mitrovica, what was your expectation? How long would the buses stay? What was the task involved? Why would they go to the barracks? Why did they not go to Sremska Mitrovica straight away?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when Bogdan Vujic left the hospital, he left the hospital before I went to see where the young soldiers got killed. I heard different testimony here, but I am sure that he left before I went off and before the observers of the European Community came. He said to me that I should stay on in the hospital to see whether there were other people there who were hiding, and that he would regulate all further questions regarding the departure of the column -- the convoy to Sremska Mitrovica. What was being awaited was to see whether there were other people left in the hospital as the wounded were being carried out. That's why they were waiting at the barracks. So what was being waited for was that, if there are some persons who were still in some cellars, a convoy could be organised and escorted by the police, the escort that would take suspects to Sremska Mitrovica. And this was regulated by the command of the Guards Brigade, when the convoys left, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, did you come to the place where the representatives of the International Red Cross were and the convoy that was supposed to evacuate the wounded? And what happened there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to this bridge, as for the radio that was on the APC that was on the bridge, because it was also from the armoured battalion, it was said that Colonel Pavkovic was looking for me. At the same time this was communicated to me by a photographer from Zastava Film called Zare; that was his nickname. He was there to record what was going on. And he said, "The colonel said that you should go to the other bridge. He said that I should tell you that if I see you." I went there, and first I saw Colonel Pavkovic there and then I saw Mr. Borsinger as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe there is no need for us to show the footage that we have already seen so many times. Could you describe for us what the reason was and why you said what you said to Mr. Borsinger during that dialogue.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was shaken by the news of the death of our three young soldiers. Then Mr. Borsinger promised that he would come at 6.00 in the morning and he didn't come. He promised that he would bring a lot of food, that he would bring food, tents, and many other things that I had asked him to bring for the people who were staying there and who had no proper accommodation. When we met, Colonel Pavkovic first complained to me that he had behaved unfairly - how should I put this? - and then when we had some conversation, he and I, he said that I should first remove the journalists, that they should not attend. And there was an enormous group of journalists there. I said, "Sir, I really don't know why we are evading journalists. Let people take pictures and let them show the world what is going on in our country." And I said to the journalists, "Feel free to record everything because this is really major suffering on the part of all of our peoples." That's what I said. I said what I said about my soldiers, and that's the way it was. And that is what the situation was at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you prohibit Mr. Borsinger or anybody else from the International Red Cross from entering the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not prohibit Mr. Borsinger or anybody else. But I got into a vehicle together with them and went to the hospital, and that can be seen on the recording as well. And I stayed with them in the hospital throughout the time while they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who carried out the evacuation of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evacuation, or rather, this convoy for the evacuation of the wounded was brought by Colonel Pavkovic and with him from officers from the 1st Military District. One was called Loncar, and I don't know -- I think he was a colonel, too, and I don't know the other names. As for the wounded being put into vehicles, Major Tesic appeared there as well and he said that Colonel Mrksic had charged him with the duty of having the wounded carried into the vehicles and establishing full order in terms of preparing the departure of the wounded from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just have to put a question to you: Do you know, in relation to the transport of these persons on the buses, whether they had any kind of military escort? And who was the military escort of these persons to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put Major Vukasinovic, my assistant for military and police affairs, in charge of that. I know that he got some soldiers from the 2nd Military Police Battalion for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From Paunovic; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the evacuation of the wounded, and we'll be looking at some footage, were there any complaints by anyone about the procedure itself? Did you ever find out that there were grievances about the way the evacuation was conducted?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout my time at the hospital, I watched, I helped, and on that day no one came to complain to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone stand in the way of the civilians present there, such as women and medical staff, preventing them from getting in touch with the ICRC people and the international observers?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no one standing in their way. If you look at the videos, you can see that everybody was perfectly free to go and talk to whomever they wanted to talk to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone stand in the way of journalists trying to get in touch with the civilians, the European monitors or any of the medical staff?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one stood in anybody else's way. They took all the pictures they wanted and pursued all of their plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll see later a particular portion where there were journalists talking to you. There were quite many journalists at the hospital as the evacuation was being conducted; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I reckon over 50 journalists and cameramen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you personally in touch with journalists? Did they ask questions about the men? Had they already been told that some men had been taken away before the crews got there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to the journalists there and they saw for themselves when the group from the barracks was returned, the group that I said should be checked again in terms of why they had been taken away. They asked me where those people had been and I told them that we'd taken some people to the barracks to be interrogated because they were crime suspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to look at a clip. It's V0001131; that is the reference. There's the B/C/S transcript for the time being, 3D060016. I gave the B/C/S to the interpreters. We don't have the English yet. So, first of all, I would like to thank the interpreters for doing their best to cover this transcript, based on our B/C/S. And then, first of all, I would like this to be marked for identification, and then once we have the English, the whole thing to be admitted. This is an excerpt from the Belgrade TV news that evening; it goes on for several minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] A little later, someone from the Red Cross headed for the Vukovar Hospital. It's some kilometres from the centre of town. I see a street leading from the centre of town to the Vukovar Hospital. To the right of this convoy, there's the police station, or rather, the MUP, the Croatian MUP station. Next to it is the municipal court. Yesterday, there was firing from that building and we saw soldiers bringing out hundreds of rifles from that building which members of the National Guard and the Croatian MUP had discarded as they were running for the hospital where some of them were hiding. This is the entrance to the hospital, and we see the representatives of the European Mission. Sljivancanin: You will allow these vehicles and these entering the hospital and the people to wear white coats with these insignia and the Red Cross signs so they can come in. Unidentified voice: The rest, nothing. The rest, nothing. Sljivancanin: Everybody should do their own job which means that nobody else would be allowed through. Journalist: These are the civilians who had fled who were in the hospital compound. Sljivancanin: We'll do the transport in that direction. Let them take this road here [ unintelligible]. Journalist: According to press agencies, there are about 400 civilians. Sljivancanin: Don't push. There will be enough room for everyone. Journalist: They are leaving on buses on their way to a holding centre; from there, to Sid, and from Sid, depending on their choice, just as on the previous days, or else they remain in their homes, if they still have roofs over their heads. Since, for the most part, they don't, they are leaving for cities in Serbia or other cities in Croatia, according to their choice. By the way, we tried to get into the hospital yesterday but our crew was not allowed inside. As we can see, for the most part, these are women and elderly people, because all the others are being screened, which means the remaining men aged between 16 and 60, because there is a suspicion that they are disguised in civilian clothes but, in actual fact, are members of the Croatian MUP and the other paramilitary units. It is precisely in the same direction that this convoy is moving across the way that there is a mass grave containing Serb bodies, being patients of the hospital who had received medical treatment, being people against whom crimes were committed. The evacuation of patients from the Vukovar Hospital is now beginning and is being monitored by the Red Cross and the European Mission. We don't know for the time being which medical centre they're being evacuated to, whether to Sremska Mitrovica or Sid, which would be the closest towns, but there will probably be a triage conducted as well. This is the inside of the hospital. Unidentified voice: [unintelligible]. Journalist: Let me repeat: There are about 420 ill and seriously wounded in the hospital. These are the first frames of what the hospital looks like inside. It is obviously overcrowded. Unidentified voice: This is the hospital. This is where you administer anaesthetics. Uniformed person: All the time throughout the last three months [unintelligible] no chance. How many operations, I don't know. Unidentified voice: What do you think about all of this? Uniformed person: I think it's dreadful. It's really, really dreadful. Unidentified voice: Will all of this end today? Uniformed person: Yes, I hope so. Journalist: That's as much as I know, given the fact that the hospital was overcrowded and there is only one room for performing surgery, and that is the room that you saw a minute ago. We must also say that a month ago, the military authorities asked the Vukovar Crisis Staff for civilians and children to be evacuated from this building. They were attempts by various international humanitarian organisations for the civilians and children to leave town, but there was a firm refusal by the Croatian authorities to allow this. This is an aggravating circumstance which seems to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are unable to work from two voices speaking at the same time. Thank you. [Voiceover] Journalist: The evacuation of the patients is underway and will be finished by evening time, as a fellow journalist Grulevic [phoen] from VRS News has told us. Unidentified voice: Don't. Stop this. Let the women out [unintelligible]. Journalist: In Vukovar Hospital, throughout these horrors, even the maternity ward kept on working. The man in a white suit is a BBC journalist. In situations like these, even journalists can be moved by what is going on and they can be found assisting civilians. This is all happening outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: On account of the exceptionally poor sound quality, the record is unreliable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this video into evidence now and the -- well, we have the interpretation. It goes with the transcript. I'm not sure what we should do about this. Perhaps we should wait for an official translation from CLSS, or perhaps we can just take it as it comes and, with the assistance of our interpreters, have this record tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I -- may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I object to that course at the moment. I thought my learned friend had indicated that he would want it to be marked for identification subject to translation. That would be my first point. The second point is this: I'm sure it's our fault, but we cannot find the video anywhere in documents disclosed to us. It may be an oversight on our behalf, but if my learned friend, over the luncheon adjournment or the next break, could tell us where it is, I would be very grateful, so we can check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you could bring that matter up when we return after the break, having, hopefully by then, resolved it. That then, of course, brings us to a convenient time for the break. We will continue at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally, just to inform the Chamber of our discussion with the OTP during the break. We submitted to the OTP a list of our documents, exhibits and documents, the 65 ter list for those that we intend to use for Mr. Sljivancanin's evidence; we provided numbers for three or four video clips. These are all numbers from their own 65 ter list exhibits, that is, proposals by the OTP, and the clip that we saw before the break is part of this video list, such as all the ones that we've been showing so far. This is OTP evidence. I can't quite nail this number for them - I'm not sure if it's in our submission - but they should be familiar with this document because it's their document. As for the transcript, my proposal is we wait for an official translation into English. So the transcript could be marked for identification, but I think the video clip should be admitted into evidence simply because it appears to be an OTP document. It's the last six and a half minutes of the clip that I marked before it was shown. The clip itself is two and a half hours long, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will receive the clip as an exhibit and the transcript will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video clip will become Exhibit 837, while the transcript will become MFI 838.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, I do not mean to lead, but in this clip we saw a man wearing a white suit and the journalist said something about him. What exactly was going on? Did you talk to that man? What else happened at the hospital during the, let me call it, evacuation of the patients?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the man in white really well. If he's monitoring what goes on here as a journalist, if he wants to know, I would like to greet him because I think that he was a great, respectful person. I believe his coverage is faithful. His name is Martin Bell. He is a journalist from England.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him at one point, and what was it about?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked that day at the hospital, because this gentleman came to see me and said that Mr. Borsinger had held a press conference near the hospital somewhere and that he spoke in exceptionally scathing terms of the JNA. Mr. Bell said, "I am an eyewitness, I have been an eyewitness to everything going on here nearly from day 1. And particularly in relation to this morning, I see that the JNA are doing their best and taking all the steps needed. I would regret such an interview becoming publicly and internationally known. I suppose you issue an official denial and I can organise your own press conference if you like." I said, "Sir, but I simply don't know what Mr. Borsinger was saying at this press conference." And he said he would hand me the very camera that was used to tape that interview and that I should follow the small screen of that camera to see what Borsinger had said at the meeting. I asked him to please wait until I had a chance to speak to my superiors. As far as I remember, I went to see Colonel Pavkovic and perhaps also the liaison officer, who was also a colonel. I think his name was Memisevic. I told them what Mr. Martin Bell had told me previously, and I asked Pavkovic to have a look and see if he could, perhaps, give an interview. Mr. Pavkovic said, "Since you were here throughout the morning, you know what was going on and you know these journalists, too. The best course of action would be for you to issue an official denial and to give the interview." I found Mr. Bell later on. They brought some interpreters. I took about half an hour, perhaps more, first to listen to Mr. Borsinger's statement. There were a lot of untruths being said. Martin Bell organised a press conference next to the hospital. A huge number of journalists assembled. I gave a brief statement for the benefit of the journalists, and the liaison officer, Colonel Memisevic was interpreting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I won't ask you exactly what you stated on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please play another video from the OTP list, V0003250. Again, we have a transcript in B/C/S which we provided to the interpreters; 3D060019. I hope that they will be successful in giving us a hand with the statement made by Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Gentlemen of the press, this is the Yugoslav People's Army. I'm proud to be at the helm of such soldiers and such officers. This army has been imposed a war and major problems are created by those who do not think well of the army. We are fighting to help every decent person and citizen of this country. I believe that you witnessed for yourself in this town of Vukovar when we pulled out and salvaged the wounded and, at the same time, the civilian population from cellars, from tunnels, from all the places where the Ustasha units were keeping them. And finally, you also saw when we finally took Vukovar, not for a single moment did any soldier, any officer, try to point his weapon or anything in order to take revenge on any civilian or any citizen that we captured here, even though they may have been on the other, opposite side, as a member of the Ustasha formations. And I'm particularly pleased because of that and I'm proud that we should be comporting ourselves with such dignity and integrity. Secondly, gentlemen, we sought to show to all journalists, to all international organisations, and to every person, everything that is happening in this city. Never did we defend anyone, prevent anyone, or advocate that anyone should not come and see what the JNA units are doing, nor are we doing that today, nor are we preventing them today from doing that in respect of the evacuation of this hospital. Although there were comrades, i.e., gentlemen from international organisations, who wanted to hold meetings behind closed doors and would not allow journalists to record everything that they wanted to tell us, then, also, I told you -- I told you that I didn't mind, that you can record everything because here, we are doing nothing clandestinely. We are only doing what all our people want in order to save all our people and all men of integrity. Certain gentlemen from the International Red Cross arrive at Vukovar and, for the most part, stroll around and observe as if they had come to review the JNA units in some sort of a control exercise. I asked them whether they were interested in the wounded, the injured, and the unattended-to young soldiers from my army. Never did they show any such interest, but they went to every length to come here, although we are caring for these wounded here. In fact, not in a single moment did they help us, the army, through the organisation of the Red Cross, for any evacuation to be undertaken or for any aid, in medicaments, in food, or in clothing, or any other items to be forthcoming to help us. We had to do it all on our own, to take proper care for about 10.000 population -- people in Vukovar, whereas they seek to portray themselves as coming here constantly as a humanitarian organisation and as being neutral. If they are neutral, if they are a humanitarian organisation, then they should not choose whom they should help but they should help all the people in Vukovar, irrespective of their national affiliation. This morning I said to one gentleman that here I was in my own homeland, in my own country, and I am the commander; I shall respect and recognise his laws and everything that he tells me when I come to his country. I offer them all conceivable hospitality, everything that I could. We provided fuel and food and accommodation for them and we took them where they wanted. But the gentlemen failed to comprehend that there is a war being waged here and that the life of every single soldier of mine is very, very important [unintelligible]. Unknown voice: [unintelligible]. Sljivancanin: These people [unintelligible] actually should have done that, irrespective of whose side they are aligned with, and no decent doctor or any individual on the medical staff should fear anything, because -- yes? Unidentified voice: There was some misunderstandings this morning with the Red Cross organisation. Has that been dealt with? Commentator: This was a question from SkyNews. Sljivancanin: No, there was no misunderstandings as far as we were concerned. No misunderstandings, gentlemen. No misunderstandings as far as we were concerned. And I have to stress, once again, that this is a war operations zone and that we are prosecuting war here and that we have to abide by the time conditions and respect the operations being conducted by JNA units. You can hear that they are still shooting here today, and we have to create conditions of security and safety for every person and every organisation coming here. And we have to have patience and we have to be patient now because we don't have peace here, but just ordinary life and this is everyday life. And you or anybody else ... [unintelligible].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is part of Mr. Sljivancanin's interview which has already become Exhibit 138 during Mr. van Lynden's evidence. Just half a minute, I think. So now I would like to suggest this entire video recording be admitted into evidence, and once we get the transcript with the official translation into English, that we tender that as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The video will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 839, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, where was Mr. Borsinger? Did you see him in that period while you were at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, before we proceed, what is going to happen about the possibility of a transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I was waiting for the answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'd better confirm that we have the transcript in the unofficial form, and I was going to propose it be treated in the same way as the previous transcript, that is, marked for identification as 840.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The B/C/S of this transcript is 3D060019, so could we please now have it marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is marked for identification with the reference 840.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you saw Mr. Borsinger and whether you prohibited him from entering the hospital. That's my second question and then let's move on.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already given you my answer; that I never prohibited him from doing that, not him, not anyone else. After this interview of mine, which I think was after 1.00 on that day, perhaps around 2.00 - I don't know the exact time - I did not meet Mr. Borsinger. I only saw him on the evening of the 21st. I assume -- well, yes, we're going to discuss that a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was in Negoslavci; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you just give us a brief description, and you mentioned that a few moments ago, when these people came, the people who were brought from the buses to the barracks, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the list that I sent to the barracks, as far as I can remember now, I think that on the list there were 20 to 24 persons, and this was handed over to me by these ladies at the hospital. This was a plain piece of paper and they wrote the names down in their own hand. Major Ljubisa Vukasinovic brought them on the bus. It was sometime after all went into the hospital, perhaps after 11.00, closer to 12.00, if I can put it that way. Then, when the Major came, he said to me -- roughly, these were his words: "Comrade Major, I had problems in the barracks because members of the Territorial Defence think that you are releasing the most notorious Ustashas, and that you did that last night at Mitnica, too. They came to around the barracks and they tried to mistreat people who I got out of the bus to return them here to the hospital, as you had asked. That is why I ask you not to send me out on such assignments." This was roughly his report to me. I asked him: "Did you return the people who were on the list?" And he said, "Yes." I asked him whether, in the barracks, whether Lieutenant Colonel Miodrag Panic was in the barracks, and he said, "Yes." I asked him whether Lukic was there, Lieutenant Colonel Lukic. He said that he was there and that a military police company was there, Captain Predojevic's company, and that the buses were safe. At that moment a group appeared, in actual fact, of members of the Territorial Defence that was brought by Miroljub Vujevic. There was this small incident there, it so happened. They expressed their revolt to me, so to speak, as to why I wanted to return those people to the buses. Vukasinovic even reacted a bit severely to one of these people and I reacted, too, so this was quickly resolved. I warned Mr. Vujevic, because I knew that he was one of the commanders in the Territorial Defence, that he should warn his people not to behave towards me in an unsoldierly way, and that he should say what it was that they wanted. He said that he knew that these were members of paramilitary formations and what kind of crimes they committed. I said to him, "All right. If you know, you will tell me and we will look into it and we will see what is true and what is not true." After that, I called some doctors from the Vukovar Hospital; I called the members of the military police. And Mr. Vujevic was there. I asked this group of people to get off the bus. I was calling out their names from that list, one by one. I asked Vujevic what he had to say to me about each and every one of these persons and what they had done wrong. That they were not wearing uniforms and that they were not carrying weapons, so I did not think that they did anything wrong and I let all these 20 people go with their families except for four. Four persons from that group said -- I remember that very well, that -- I mean they themselves admitted, nobody forced them to say this, that at the gasoline station in Vukovar, they killed some people and they said who it was that they had killed. And I said to their families and to them that they had to go to be interrogated in prison. And I asked Major Vukasinovic that these four be returned again to the group of suspects that were being sent to prison, and I released the rest. As for that case, as for that case, that is how it was resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have some exhibits here, 331 and 333, and we are not going to place them on the screen now. You saw them. They say that the convoy with the wounded left the hospital around 1430 hours. I'm going to ask you the following: Were you there when the convoy left the hospital, and does that actually correspond to what your memory is in terms of when the convoy left the hospital? Just be brief.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there when the convoy left and I think that the hour is correct, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, maybe, some details? We heard Mara Bucko testify before this Court, when you suggested to the medical staff that they stay on and work in the hospital, even then.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even then, and a few times during the course of the day, at the intervention of Dr. Ivezic, and some other doctors who decided to stay on working at the hospital, I asked some of them to stay on and work in the hospital, some of them who wanted to leave. But many left, many did not want to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to put three questions to you. Please answer briefly and then we will go on. During the course of that day, in the period when these buses were in barracks, did you come to the barracks at any point in time, and did you enter the barracks in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. On that day, I never entered the barracks in Vukovar until night-time. At night-time, in the evening of the 20th of November, I was at the gate of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever at Velepromet in that period, on that day?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, during the course of that day, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that day, evening, or night, at any point in time, were you in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, I was not at Ovcara either during the day or during the night, on that day, the 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said a few moments ago, about the barracks in Vukovar -- rather, who was the commander of the barracks, and within whose area of responsibility was the Vukovar barracks on the day of the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know - but I would kindly like to ask that we use documents more because maybe I'm making mistakes - the commander of the garrison was Lieutenant Colonel Lukic. But I saw an order here as well that was presented to the Court that, on the 18th of November or before that, that Major Adem Bajic was commander of the barracks, appointed commander of the barracks, and the area around the barracks. So out of these two, one was it, but it is hard for me to say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, who provided security of the barracks in Vukovar at that time, and what comprised this security?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to all military regulations, the commander of barracks is responsible for the security of the barracks. And the security consisted of all the members who were there, especially the personnel who were assigned to carry out those security duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to the testimony we heard from quite a few witnesses before this Court, the period when the buses left barracks is between 1330 and 1430 hours, to put it in general terms. I'm going to put a few questions to you in relation to the indictment and in relation to this topic. Mr. Sljivancanin, did you personally supervise the detention of detainees in barracks during about two hours while the members of the TO were exposing them to threats and psychological provocations?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite incorrect. On that day, I was not in the barracks and there are exact recordings, including video recordings, as to where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more thing, Mr. Sljivancanin. During that triage, during the search, and while these persons were being taken away, did you see whether in that hospital, within the hospital compound, by the buses, there were any volunteers, territorials?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really did not observe any such thing. I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard before this Court evidence to the effect that a meeting of the government of the Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem government was held at that time. I'm going to ask you whether you attended that government session at any point then.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for a moment was I present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you something and then please answer me then and then we're going to hear the content. When did you hear, and from whom, that the government meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I heard that the government session was held was on the evening of the 20th, when I returned to my building in Negoslavci. I heard this from Captain Srecko Borisavljevic and later at the command post from Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During this period when the buses left and up until when you left to Negoslavci - and you will tell us when this happened, if you can specify this - where were you and what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the buses left, I went to the shelter that I described to you, near the hospital, where the demining had been completed. So I toured the entire shelter and that's where one of my security officers was, Captain Karanfilov. I tasked him with collecting the equipment that was in that shelter. And since the security administration had asked me to have this done, I told them to have this taken to the security administration in Belgrade. I believe that immediately after that he left. I know that he took this and that this equipment did, indeed, reach the security administration. Night was already falling by then, by the time I returned from that shelter. I went to see Dr. Ivezic in hospital, because there were other wounded persons who were left in the hospital and we agreed that he should prepare them to be evacuated on the following day. Then, the hospital staff offered to have a cup of coffee. I sat with them for about an hour or so, perhaps even more. We had coffee and they told me what they had experienced there before in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took my vehicle from there to the command post or to Negoslavci. Passing by the barracks, I stopped at the gate of the barracks and that's where I saw Captain Mladen Predojevic -- Captain Blagoje Predojevic, commander of the company of military police. I cannot be sure as to whether there was somebody else there with him. Maybe there were some other officers there, too, but he was there for sure. It's really hard for me to say whether there was anyone else. In any event, Predojevic roughly said the following to me: that the evacuation from the barracks had taken place as planned, that the soldiers were resting now, that his company was providing security, and that no one was there any longer except for the soldiers, and that this is the first night after so many sleepless nights where they can get some better rest. I gave him a bit of advice there. I told him to take care of the safety and security of the soldiers, I told him about the death of the soldiers the previous night, and I proceeded along the road to Negoslavci. As I was passing by Velepromet, perhaps I stopped at Velepromet, but really it is hard for me to say all these things now. If I stopped there, it was peaceful over there, too. I don't remember that detail. And I came to my building in the village of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you find anyone there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found Srecko Borisavljevic. When I went to see Predojevic, I was looking for him, too, at the barracks, and he said he had gone before I had arrived in Negoslavci. So I called Major Vukasinovic as well. Major Vukasinovic told me this: When he had returned those people from the hospital and when he arrived at the barracks, the last thing Predojevic told him was that an order had arrived from the commander that those people should be taken to Ovcara, and that he had taken those people to Ovcara, which surprised me. He found the other people from barracks there and members of the TO, including Miroljub Vujevic. He said they were behaving - how should I put it? - violently. He warned Miroljub that this was no way to go about this, or that's at least what he told me. He restored order to that scene and he said that all those people went into a hangar where the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade secured them. The brigade's Chief of Staff, Lieutenant Colonel Panic, was there, too. After this, he went back to the command post and informed Colonel Mrksic about all of this. He said Mrksic told him nothing. After that, Srecko Borisavljevic told me this: He said that there had been a government meeting at Velepromet, or that's what it was now called, the Baranja and Western Srem SAO, or what have you. When they came there for the meeting, Srecko opposed this. He refused to let them inside Velepromet. After a while, Lieutenant Colonel Matko Petrovic appeared. He was from the moral guidance organ. He conveyed to him the order and approval that Colonel Mrksic had granted for this meeting to be held at Velepromet. Srecko said that he had no further part in this, but he knew that Colonel Bogdan Vujic had attended the meeting. Bogdan Vujic later told him that at the government meeting the decision had been taken for the suspects who had been taken from the hospital to the barracks to be handed over to the government of Western Srem and Slavonia so that they could be exchanged for captured Serbs. Srecko asked him who had taken that decision and Mr. Vujic apparently told him, "The powers that be." This is what I was told by my two security clerks when I reached Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Borisavljevic say anything about the previous evening at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me about that, too. He said the previous evening there had been a triage as planned and Colonel Vujic was in charge while he was helping. At one point in time, a drunken TO member appeared. I think he mentioned the name, too, but the name escapes me and it's very difficult to remember what it was. This man was sent away. However, there was a distinct possibility that more such people would appear at Velepromet. I then told Srecko that he should go back to the barracks that evening, that he should tell the barracks commander about this, and that he should tell him, as well as the military police company commander, that I said that should this man turn up again, they should arrest him. And also to check whether, at Velepromet, there were other such people that were not put up properly. If so, he should ask the commander for those people to be taken to spend the night at the barracks until they could be sent to wherever it was they were going in order to avoid any further mistreatment or harassment occurring. The next day, Srecko told me that he had done what I had told him to do and that he had spoken to the barracks commander. But he also found out, apparently, that this man was from a detachment under the command of Milan Lancuzanin and that the commander had already sent him away from the area of combat operations that same day. This man was a volunteer and therefore we had no power to arrest him, or probably that was the very reason he had sent him away, because we were about to arrest that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Colonel Mrksic's command to see him, and when?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the meeting with these officers, the one I told you about here, I went to the command post and called in on Colonel Mrksic. As far as I can recall at this time, Colonel Mrksic was sitting there, as was Lieutenant Colonel Panic, I think one of the operations officers, but I really cannot remember everything, and there was definitely an officer sitting at the signals desk. I briefly reported on what was basically happening with the hospital. The Colonel told me that he had also been informed by Colonel Pavkovic and that he was in constant contact with him. We didn't discuss that very much. As far as I remember, he told me this: "We have completed our missions. The Guards Brigade is pulling out to get some rest. All the commitments in this area will be taken over by the 80th Motorised Brigade and the Vukovar TO detachment. Today, a government meeting was held of the Baranja, Slavonia, and Western Srem government at Velepromet. They will now start setting up civilian authorities. They also took charge of a group of suspects from the hospital who had been brought to the barracks in order to later be exchanged for captured Serbs." He also said that he would be off to a meeting in Belgrade, a meeting with the Federal Secretary. Having returned from that meeting, he would be making further decisions about what the brigade would be doing next. He told me that the following day, the 21st of November, 1991, there would be a press conference at the Vukovar barracks, and that Lieutenant Colonel Panic would be in charge of that. He said that the next morning, as soon as I'd rested, I should give Lieutenant Colonel Panic a hand to make sure the whole thing went smoothly and safely. He also said that General Vasiljevic had asked to speak to me urgently, that I should get in touch as quickly as possible, and that was the end of our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I immediately used the services of that signals officer to speak to General Vasiljevic in the security department. All these days I've been racking my brains trying to remember whether it was Mr. Vasiljevic that I spoke to or a colonel who was on duty at the security administration. I seem to his name, Radojevic. So it will much sooner have been the colonel that I spoke to at the time. But be that as it may, he told me why Vasiljevic had asked to speak to me and wanted to see me. He said that the general had ordered that first night that he came to see me, for me to gather all the documents that I had taken from Marin Vidic and from other ZNG men and the hideout used by the commander of the ZNG, and send them immediately to the security administration. I told the colonel that the documents were already on their way to Belgrade and that they would be receiving those either during that same night or perhaps the following morning, and that was the end of that conversation. I then went back to the building where I was billeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do next that evening?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was moving towards that building, I met some officers, Zvorcan, perhaps, or someone. It was the TV news time, the evening news time, and someone told me that some coverage from Vukovar had been announced to cover what had transpired on that day. And they also said they would be showing footage of me. This would be after the evening news but it was something that was announced during the actual TV news. He came up with the idea that we should see this programme together. I went to that house but there was no TV. There was a TV set at Colonel Mrksic's command post or at the press centre, but if you used the generator, or as soon as there was electricity, you were able to watch TV. That evening, we were able to watch TV and I watched all this footage from Vukovar that was aired that night. This went on until 11.00 in the evening, I believe. I also saw the footage that I've just seen; first of all, my talk with Borsinger at the bridge, and then the last footage that was shown. That programme was the footage from the press conference organized by Martin Bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, I've asked you about Ovcara, haven't I? Did you personally send anyone to Ovcara that day, that evening, that night?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't send anyone to Ovcara that day, that evening, that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that any of the officers from your own security organ, with the exception of Vukasinovic, which is something you've described for us, went to Ovcara that evening?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that no one went because I knew the whereabouts of all my officers. And I still know - and I can tell you - Vukasinovic was right there in Negoslavci. He was a town commander. Srecko Borisavljevic was off to the barracks on the business that I had charged him with. Karanfilov was in the process of bringing documents from the shelter to the security administration. Karan was in Sremska Mitrovica with Captain Bozic, about taking Marin Vidic, Bili; Vesna Bosanac; Njavro; and that man from the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about any military policemen from the Guards Brigade being at Ovcara that night?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that but I wasn't in a position to check where the MPs were. That was something for the military police commander to do. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase something that the Prosecutor alleges in the indictment. Did you tell anyone to confer the powers and the orders --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand Mr. Lukic's question.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that would be utter nonsense. There was no chain of command making it possible for anyone to carry out an order like that, nor was I authorised to carry out any such orders, nor was I authorised to interfere with the area of responsibility of another unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies to the interpreters. I will try to ask this question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question was: Did you tell anyone, did you personally convey to anyone, to inform or to convey or to order that the Ovcara order should be retracted? You've provided the answer. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I say it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that will be necessary. Thank you. The next day, there was the press conference. I wouldn't -- well, maybe a couple of words. But if you can tell me what you described. Your meeting again with Borsinger, when was it? And, briefly, what was it like? What was the level of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next morning, at about 7.00, the 21st of November, 1991, at about 7.00, I reported to Lieutenant Colonel Panic and was off to the Vukovar barracks. I was there when the press conference took place. I'm not sure about the time, but I think it went on until about 12.00 or 1.00 p.m. After that, I was tasked with taking the journalists - and I'm not sure who was in charge of this - around Vukovar to show them all the places where we had previously located shelters, bunkers, fortified buildings, and all of the stuff that had gone on. I remained with them until nightfall. There were other officers with us. At one point I received a message via the radio that I had on me all the time that people from the ICRC were looking for me. The message came through from Negoslavci. I asked who this was, who these people were who were looking for me, and they said Mr. Borsinger was trying to track me down. I said they should tell him that I was willing to talk to him and that it was possible for us to talk but not before 1900 hours that evening, if that was convenient for him, on account of my other commitments. The answer came back that he had agreed. So we met, we had dinner together, on the 21st of November, 1991, at 1900 hours, in Vukovar. And there were three our people from the ICRC accompanying him. We had dinner for over two hours, and we talked. The gentleman, so to speak, apologised, saying that he had not been aware of our soldiers being killed. He said he was sorry for any misunderstanding that may have occurred between us, that we were always respectful in the way we treated them. I took that at face value and that brought our meeting to an end. It was a friendly and cordial end to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no questions left about Vukovar but I do have some questions left for Witness Sljivancanin. I wanted to finish today, although I wasn't able to. I also want to ask some questions about what happened after Vukovar and complete my examination-in-chief.

utterances.text: We will adjourn now, Mr. Lukic, to resume on Monday, in the afternoon, at 2.15.
